source.title: The Hidden Subgroup Problem - Review and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: What exact quantum circuit construction, rather than only an approximation, can compute the quantum Fourier transform F_N for an odd cyclic group Z_N in time polynomial in log N?
accepted.context_brief: Exact QFT for odd cyclic groups

evidence.quote: It is not currently known how to construct an exact QFT for odd cyclic groups, so this is as good as it (currently) gets.

accepted.question_text: Can one design an efficient quantum algorithm for the hidden subgroup problem over the symmetric group S_n, so that the standard reduction from graph automorphism and graph isomorphism to HSP over S_n yields a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for graph isomorphism?

evidence.quote: The main open problem in the field is finding an efficient quantum algorithm for the symmetric group Sn, which would yield an elusive (for over 30 years) efficient algorithm for determining graph isomorphism.
This shows f can be used in the standard quantum Fourier sampling algorithm to find generators for H. If this can be done efficiently is an open question.

accepted.question_text: Is there a choice of basis for the irreducible representations of S_n or other nonabelian groups that makes quantum Fourier sampling informative enough to solve the hidden subgroup problem efficiently, despite the known failure of random-basis choices?

evidence.quote: For example, it is known the standard method cannot solve the HSP over Sn if the basis choice is random - it will take a clever basis choice for the irreducibles to obtain an efficient algorithm.
Yet there is hope that a clever basis choice for the irreducible representations might turn this around.

accepted.question_text: If quantum Fourier sampling is not sufficient for the symmetric-group hidden subgroup problem, is there a different quantum algorithmic approach, not based on Fourier sampling, that can still solve the problem efficiently and thereby lead to an efficient graph-isomorphism algorithm?

evidence.quote: A second possibility, also seemingly remote, is finding a new quantum algorithm which does the trick, avoiding Fourier sampling completely.

accepted.question_text: For which finite groups can the information-theoretic ability to distinguish hidden subgroups with only polynomially many oracle queries be converted into a full polynomial-time quantum algorithm that actually outputs subgroup generators, rather than requiring exponential classical postprocessing?

evidence.quote: However, this reconstruction is harder in the nonabelian case. For example, Ettinger, Høyer, and Knill [46] have shown only polynomially many calls in log |G| to the oracle distinguishes subgroups for any group G information theoretically, but it is currently unknown how to extract generators for H without exponential classical postprocessing time.
Unfortunately, deducing H from the resulting quantum state requires exponential classical time, and it is still open for which groups this can be reduced to a polynomial time quantum algorithm.

accepted.question_text: For black-box group algorithms whose current proofs use only the abelian quantum Fourier transform, does replacing that step with genuinely nonabelian quantum Fourier transforms lead to stronger algorithmic results or more efficient hidden-subgroup procedures?

evidence.quote: A question remains: the above proofs only use the abelian QFT to get the results. Does using the nonabelian QFTs give better results?
